In gene sets discovered in ‘omics data, GPT-4 names were more informative than gene set enrichment, with supporting statements and citations that largely verified in human review. The ability to rapidly synthesize common gene functions positions LLMs as valuable functional genomics assistants.

papers.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

papers.title: Glycosyltransferases: Mining, engineering and applications in biosynthesis of glycosylated plant natural products
papers.abstract: UDP-Glycosyltransferases (UGTs) catalyze the transfer of nucleotide-activated sugars to specific acceptors, among which the GT1 family enzymes are well-known for their function in biosynthesis of natural product glycosides. Elucidating GT function represents necessary step in metabolic engineering of aglycone glycosylation to produce drug leads, cosmetics, nutrients and sweeteners. In this review, we systematically summarize the phylogenetic distribution and catalytic diversity of plant GTs. We also discuss recent progress in the identification of novel GT candidates for synthesis of plant natural products (PNPs) using multi-omics technology and deep learning predicted models. We also highlight recent advances in rational design and directed evolution engineering strategies for new or improved GT functions. Finally, we cover recent breakthroughs in the application of GTs for microbial biosynthesis of some representative glycosylated PNPs, including flavonoid glycosides (fisetin 3-O-glycosides, astragalin, scutellarein 7-O-glucoside), terpenoid glycosides (rebaudioside A, ginsenosides) and polyketide glycosides (salidroside, polydatin).

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
papers.abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children's Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

papers.title: Generalized biomolecular modeling and design with RoseTTAFold All-Atom
papers.abstract: Deep-learning methods have revolutionized protein structure prediction and design but are presently limited to protein-only systems. We describe RoseTTAFold All-Atom (RFAA), which combines a residue-based representation of amino acids and DNA bases with an atomic representation of all other groups to model assemblies that contain proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, metals, and covalent modifications, given their sequences and chemical structures. By fine-tuning on denoising tasks, we developed RFdiffusion All-Atom (RFdiffusionAA), which builds protein structures around small molecules. Starting from random distributions of amino acid residues surrounding target small molecules, we designed and experimentally validated, through crystallography and binding measurements, proteins that bind the cardiac disease therapeutic digoxigenin, the enzymatic cofactor heme, and the light-harvesting molecule bilin.

papers.title: Regional Signals Matter: Rethinking Global Pooling for mRNA Foundation Models
papers.abstract: RNA foundation models with diverse architectures have shown promise for learning representations of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences. However, existing benchmarks commonly reduce token-level embeddings to transcript-level representations through global mean pooling before fitting a downstream probe. This aggregation does not explicitly preserve the identities of biologically distinct mRNA regions. Consequently, signals associated with short regulatory regions may be diluted, confounding assessments of representation quality with the information preserved by the readout. We introduce an architecture-agnostic, region-aware readout that separately averages embeddings within the 5$'$ untranslated region (UTR), coding sequence, and 3$'$ UTR and concatenates the resulting representations for linear probing. We reproduce mRNABench evaluations for 20 frozen models from 18 families, with a median absolute score difference of 0.0009 across 380 model--dataset--target evaluations published for 19 models, and construct a region-aware benchmark using the same models, tasks, and splits. Relative to global mean pooling, region-aware pooling increases Pearson correlation, averaged across the 20 models, by 11--25\% on translation and stability tasks, with no statistically significant decreases detected for any model on the regression tasks. On classification tasks, relative changes in the area under the precision--recall curve range from $-3\%$ to $+11\%$. Boundary randomization and displacement generally reduce performance, while dimensionality-matched and sequence-composition controls indicate that the gains are not explained solely by increased feature dimensionality, region length, or guanine--cytosine (GC) content. Learned attention pooling approaches region-aware performance only when supplied with one query per region. In silico perturbations reveal stronger sensitivity to upstream AUGs (uAUGs) and their Kozak context, while analyses of endogenous transcripts show approximately threefold greater recovery of length- and GC-adjusted uAUG-associated differences than global-mean probes. Both readouts capture codon optimality. Model rankings averaged over the regression tasks remain largely stable, while within a task models move by several places. Our region-aware benchmark therefore provides a biologically structured and complementary evaluation of mRNA foundation models, revealing regulatory information that is less accessible to linear probes after global mean pooling. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/Sanford-Labs/rnaregionpooling

papers.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

papers.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

papers.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
papers.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: TMCells: A topic-based probabilistic framework for interpretable metacell construction in single-cell data.
papers.abstract: Metacells have emerged as an important analytical strategy for addressing the computational barriers posed by the scale and complexity of large-scale single-cell omics data, while preserving biologically relevant information and improving analytical interpretability. However, existing metacell inference methods usually have limited biological interpretability, rely on deterministic assignments that insufficiently capture continuous state transitions, and may lose potential biological signals due to prior feature selection or dimensionality reduction. We propose TMCells, an interpretable metacell identification algorithm based on a probabilistic generative framework. TMCells introduces the concept of topic modeling and uses a Gaussian mixture model as the prior for topic distribution, defining metacells as statistical distribution centers in the latent topic space. By modeling the cell generation process, TMCells enables the simultaneous learning of topic representations and metacell partitions in an end-to-end manner, capturing the continuity and uncertainty in cell state transitions. TMCells effectively identifies high-quality metacells, eliminating technical noise while preserving the original biological heterogeneity, thereby enhancing downstream analyses such as differential expression, rare cell type identification, and trajectory inference. Furthermore, TMCells provides an intuitive interpretation of cellular heterogeneity through latent topics associated with biologically meaningful regulatory programs, offering a generative perspective for dissecting regulatory dynamics during cell-state transitions. The TMCells along with detailed documentation is freely available at https://github.com/Jinsl-lab/TMCells with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24198840. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
papers.abstract: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

papers.title: Computable Genomes: A Layered Computational Framework for Non-Coding DNA and Cellular Behavior
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have catalogued tens of thousands of trait-associated loci, most of them in non-coding DNA, yet for most loci the path from nucleotide to phenotype remains correlational. We propose a layered computational decomposition of the genome as a complement to data-driven approaches: sequence as formal language, sequence as information-bearing signal, mobile elements as runtime, compilation to interaction networks through thermodynamic and rule-based models, and execution as cellular and multicellular dynamics. Each layer is defined by its inputs, outputs and formalisms, and we set out where the frame breaks down, including the looseness of algorithmic-information estimates, the triviality of universality results and the failure of string grammars at the chromatin level. Synthetic-biology platforms serve as tests of whether the layers compose, and genomic foundation models and the AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicts effects for all nine billion possible single-nucleotide variants, serve as oracles whose coverage and limits we map onto the framework. We state five falsifiable predictions and test the first, that sequence compressibility carries information about regulatory function beyond composition and conservation, on 38,556 single-nucleotide variants from a saturation-mutagenesis reporter assay of 21 regulatory elements. In a pooled model, local compressibility is associated with measured effect size (standardized {beta} = -0.030, p = 0.0014). The association roughly halves under full control for base composition, loses significance when composition, motif and noise adjustments are combined under locus-level inference (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.11), and averages zero within loci (random-effects {beta} = -0.0003, p = 0.90). The prediction is therefore not supported at the variant level in these data, which bound the effect a genome-wide test should expect. The argument is not that the genome "is" a program, but that treating it as one supplies formal tools whose predictions can be checked.

papers.title: CIRCA learns identifiable cell- and niche-level programs and their interactions with tissue pathology from spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Interactions among cells and their local microenvironments shape tissue organization and function, while their dysregulation can contribute to disease. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), the complex responses of glial cells and neurons to amyloid-{beta} pathology can both mitigate and exacerbate neuronal injury. Spatial transcriptomics enables investigation of these relationships in situ, but recovering interpretable transcriptional programs and their interactions from spatial transcriptomics remains challenging, in part because conventional nonlinear models are non-identifiable. Here we present CIRCA (Causal Interaction Representation for Cellular Architectures), a self-supervised causal representation learning framework that jointly learns identifiable cell- and neighborhood-level transcriptional programs and the directed interactions among them under explicit assumptions. It can also be extended to incorporate additional modalities such as pathology. Benchmarked against five existing methods across seven cell-resolution datasets, CIRCA achieved the highest biological accuracy in six and the highest overall score in all five multi-section datasets, while recovering higher-order anatomical organization. In an AD mouse model, incorporating amyloid-{beta} pathology revealed four region-specific plaque niches enriched for microglia. Plaque-associated microglia shared a core disease-associated response whose strength varied by region, and AD genetic risk was preferentially enriched in hippocampal and cortical plaque-associated microglia. Reproducible latent factors linked to cell-level amyloid burden separated phagocytic from inflammatory microglial programs. Applied to a human colorectal cancer dataset, CIRCA resolved patient-specific tumor niches, conserved stromal remodeling niches, and distinct macrophage states, highlighting its versatility. Together, these results establish CIRCA as a methodological advance over existing approaches, enabling deeper insights into tissue organization and the molecular dependencies linking cells to their local environments.

papers.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

papers.title: Measuring the information budget of cross-target antibody affinity generalization: a robust cross-target wall, and why structure reaches developability but not affinity
papers.abstract: Structure-based machine learning is widely expected to advance antibody engineering, yet it is unclear how far affinity predictions transfer to new targets, and why. We introduce a noise-corrected, censoring-aware estimator of the cross-target transfer ceiling, {rho}max = {surd}(T/(T+I)), which separates a transferable antibody-intrinsic component (T) from a non-transferable target-specific interaction (I). On deterministic synthetic ground truth the estimator recovers the noise-free ceiling to {+/-} 0.0003, whereas the naive sum-of-squares estimator is biased downward by measurement noise. Applying it from synthetic to real systems, the transferable budget is small, and on real neutralization panels it is not an artefact: the target-specific interaction survives noise and censoring correction. It is strongly regime-dependent, with a two-tier structure: predicting a novel antibody from sequence alone (the design setting) reaches a lower ceiling ({rho} {approx} 0.44 on real breadth data) than ranking a characterized one ({rho} {approx} 0.59), even with a strong protein language model. Synthetic oracles also overstate transferability: an oracle scored on real predicted structures carries about half the budget of a matched synthetic lattice (0.45 vs. 0.81), and real neutralization and escape panels sit well below the synthetic ceiling (0.32-0.68). Under leakage-free antigen-cluster splits, cross-target affinity ranking across every method family collapses to this budget, while within a sampled target a structure-based graph network ranks affinity above off-the-shelf FoldX and GearBind (within-complex Spearman 0.55), and structural surface descriptors predict a surface-driven developability property (hydrophobic aggregation) where sequence-dominated properties (humanness, charge-driven self-association) do not benefit. A controlled ablation attributes the residual within-target signal to the antibody alone: dropping the antigen from the structural model leaves it essentially unchanged (interface {Delta} {rho} between -0.01 and +0.02 across four panels), so for this model the paratope-epitope interface adds no ranking signal over the antibody alone. Models climb toward the budget within a target -- via a measure-then-rank operating mode that recovers top binders 6-8 times more efficiently than random once a target has been sampled -- but none crosses it.

papers.title: Multi-omics profiling links epigenetic and lncRNA changes to early human endochondral ossification priming
papers.abstract: Differentiation programs remain incompletely understood across stem cell types, including for human bone marrow mesenchymal stromal/stem (BM-MSCs) cells, a heterogenous population orchestrating bone formation and establishing a functional hematopoietic niche in the bone marrow. BM-MSCs form and repair bone through the evolutionarily conserved process of endochondral ossification (EO), initiated by deposition of a transient cartilage template subsequently remodeled into bone and bone marrow tissues. Despite their considerable potential for skeletal regeneration, the early molecular and cellular events underlying BM-MSCs commitment to EO remain elusive. To overcome donor dependent variability in chondrogenic potential that limits mechanistic studies, we here exploit OssiGel as a potent chondro-inductive extracellular matrix offering robust recapitulation of EO by BMMSCs. Through multi-omics profiling of OssiGel-primed BM-MSCs, we identify rapid chromatin remodeling at chondrogenic loci as concomitant for lineage commitment. The emergence of a chondro-progenitor population is detected as early as 3 days in vivo and correlates with successful EO recapitulation. Mechanistically, we identify LINC02511 as novel enhancer-associated element involved in the onset of EO. We confirm presence of LINC02511 in human skeletal atlases, and its CRISPR-mediated silencing significantly impaired EO. By integrating human tissue engineering strategies with single cell multi-omics profiling, our study provides a framework for deciphering BM-MSCs fate decisions, highlighting the role of enhancer and non-coding elements as key determinants of early lineage specification. These findings advance our understanding of BM-MSCs biology and will prompt their translational exploitation in regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

papers.title: Brain disorder mechanisms and therapeutic targets identified from developmental, cell-specific gene regulation
papers.abstract: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain.

papers.title: PlantPAN 5.0: updated database for integrating multiomics evidence and exploring multilayered transcriptional regulatory networks in plants.
papers.abstract: Plant Promoter Analysis Navigator (PlantPAN) 5.0 (https://plantpan.itps.ncku.edu.tw/) is an integrated multiomics resource for investigating plant cis-regulatory elements and transcriptional regulatory networks. This release expands genome annotations and promoter sequences to 240 species and provides 71 040 transcription factor (TF) annotations and 7762 nonredundant binding matrices. Its companion database, PCBase 3.0, substantially expands ChIP-seq data and newly incorporates ATAC-seq, bisulfite-sequencing, and four Hi-C-based chromatin interaction datasets for Arabidopsis thaliana. The new Differential Analysis function enables comparison of TF binding, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation across conditions. The redesigned Promoter Analysis interface provides TF family-level statistics, with a Pattern Overview panel integrating TF-binding site (TFBS) densities, plant DNA large language model-predicted open-chromatin regions, CpG-rich regions, and tandem repeats. Two new modules are introduced: (i) Transcriptome Regulatory Analysis and Coexpression, where candidate regulatory TFs and shared cis-elements in gene sets are prioritized through differential expression and coexpression analysis, and (ii) Interaction Topology Analysis for Chromatin and TFs, where chromatin interaction regions are integrated to reveal potentially coregulated genes and their shared TFs and predicted TFBSs. A Dockerized package enables large-scale local promoter analyses, with data privacy. Therefore, PlantPAN 5.0 is a comprehensive framework for discovering plant transcriptional regulatory mechanisms.

papers.title: DNA language model GROVER learns sequence context in the human genome
papers.abstract: Deep-learning models that learn a sense of language on DNA have achieved a high level of performance on genome biological tasks. Genome sequences follow rules similar to natural language but are distinct in the absence of a concept of words. We established byte-pair encoding on the human genome and trained a foundation language model called GROVER (Genome Rules Obtained Via Extracted Representations) with the vocabulary selected via a custom task, next- k -mer prediction. The defined dictionary of tokens in the human genome carries best the information content for GROVER. Analysing learned representations, we observed that trained token embeddings primarily encode information related to frequency, sequence content and length. Some tokens are primarily localized in repeats, whereas the majority widely distribute over the genome. GROVER also learns context and lexical ambiguity. Average trained embeddings of genomic regions relate to functional genomics annotation and thus indicate learning of these structures purely from the contextual relationships of tokens. This highlights the extent of information content encoded by the sequence that can be grasped by GROVER. On fine-tuning tasks addressing genome biology with questions of genome element identification and protein–DNA binding, GROVER exceeds other models’ performance. GROVER learns sequence context, a sense for structure and language rules. Extracting this knowledge can be used to compose a grammar book for the code of life.

papers.title: Decoding antibody-antigen recognition: the BL8 language and its application in calibrating deep learning predictions
papers.abstract: Antibodies are central to immunology and therapeutics, and understanding how they recognize antigens is essential to rational drug design. This recognition depends on the interplay of interface geometry, physicochemical interactions, sequence context, and complementarity-determining region (CDR) conformation. However, traditional analyses often oversimplify this complexity, which becomes particularly problematic when evaluating the massive and frequently overconfident structural hypotheses generated by modern deep learning models. Here, we introduce BL8, an interpretable, eight-view structural language that comprehensively parameterizes interfaces across topology, shape, interaction, CDR conformation, flexibility, interfacial area, amino-acid-pair composition, and sequence background. Using 15,396 experimental interface records from the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab), we built a fixed reference atlas containing 1,498 discrete BL8 signatures. The atlas shows that natural interfaces occupy a diverse, long-tailed structural space in which similar geometric scaffolds can be associated with different chemical and sequence features. Furthermore, we projected 28,501 predicted complexes involving programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), generated using AlphaFold 3 (AF3), Protenix-v2, and OpenDDE, into the reference space. Acting as a robust underlying calibration layer, BL8 successfully decoupled physical viability from native confidence illusions, revealing cross-target hallucinations and filtering out 15.3% to 20.1% of highly deceptive false-positive predictions. Crucially, by benchmarking distinct generative behaviors across models, it enabled the extraction of highly reliable, multi-model consensus out-of-distribution binding paradigms. Together, BL8 bridges foundational biophysics with large-scale computational predictions, providing an essential benchmarking framework for discovering novel mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: STARgrid - an open end-to-end pipeline for Visium HD
papers.abstract: Grid-based spatial transcriptomics quantifies expression by counting reads, assigning them to genes and, from their barcodes, to capture locations on a grid, which is registered to a microscope image. For Visium HD, only the vendor's Space Ranger performs all these steps, and its licences prohibit redistributing it or software derived from it. We present STARgrid, an open-source, end-to-end, agent-ready pipeline from Visium HD FASTQ files and images to count matrices registered to the tissue. Its counts agree closely with Space Ranger's (gene-total correlations at least 0.9989); it runs 2.0-3.4 times faster and counts 1.9-7.6% more molecules. Unlike Space Ranger, STARgrid always assigns each read to the closest-matching barcode, which gives 0.8-1.1% of matched reads a different location, mostly where adjacent-row barcodes overlap, and places another 2.9-4.6%. This choice and settling ties for each molecule from all its reads are the largest source of added molecules. Around nuclei, counts follow a reproducible pattern: more molecules in a ring just around each nucleus, usually with a dip under it. STARgrid registers the image by matching the nuclei to the whole pattern with the correlation ratio, even where the dip is weak or absent. On lung tissue imaged by Xenium on the same section, this places the nuclei where Xenium does or one capture location away. The added molecules behave as signal: they are inside cells almost as often as the others, and bring 15 of 20 abundant cancer genes closer to Xenium on an adjacent section (P = 0.0414).

papers.title: DeepCDS: Ab initio coding sequence prediction in prokaryotic metagenomic short reads
papers.abstract: Accurate coding sequence prediction in short prokaryotic metagenomic sequences, such as Illumina reads, remains challenging due to sequence fragmentation, unknown sequence origins, and sequencing errors. Here we introduce DeepCDS, a deep learning-based ab initio coding sequence predictor trained on short prokaryotic sequences with and without simulated Illumina-like sequencing errors. DeepCDS integrates embeddings from the protein language model ESM-2 with nucleotide-level information to predict complete and partial coding sequences. Benchmarking on 215 phylogenetically diverse prokaryotic organisms demonstrates that DeepCDS consistently outperforms well-established and widely used methods in coding sequence detection across sequence lengths from 75 to 1,000 base pairs, including improved identification of both canonical and non-canonical start codons as well as stop codons, and greater robustness to different sequencing error profiles. DeepCDS also recovers more coding sequences from functionally uncharacterized genes and remains operational on sequences shorter than existing tools support. We additionally evaluate DeepCDS on a simulated metagenomic dataset from the Critical Assessment of Metagenome Interpretation initiative, where it likewise achieves the strongest performance among tested tools, and on a real human gut metagenome, where its predictions are more frequently supported by known proteins. These findings suggest that amino acid-level context, here provided by a protein language model, contributes complementary information for nucleotide-level coding sequence detection, especially at very short lengths. Ultimately, DeepCDS may help uncover the functional potential of the vast microbial diversity that remains genomically uncharacterized.

papers.title: Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.

papers.title: Chimera: Cross-Species Single-Cell Generative Modeling of Expression Deployment Relative to Protein Conservation
papers.abstract: A protein's sequence says what a gene could do in another species; the cells of that species say what it does there. Comparative genomics measures the first. Chimera measures the second, a gene's deployment, on the same genes and reports the difference. It aligns single-cell atlases across species in one generative model and returns, for every one-to-one ortholog, the evidence in the counts for a shared expression pattern, and {Delta}[a], the position of that evidence above or below what the protein's identity predicts. This difference is not sequence constraint under another name: across eight tissues, protein identity tracks dN/dS, whereas {Delta}[a] tracks neither. A gene therefore has two coordinates, not one, and the second can contradict the first: spermatocyte genes such as ZPBP2 keep their stage pattern on less conserved proteins, in eight held-out species, whereas conserved hepatocyte enzymes such as ALAS1 share their pattern but not their level. More broadly, genes of specialized cells sit above what their proteins predict in 23 of 24 cohorts, and approved drug targets do so more often than matched genes. Even among nearly identical proteins, where sequence can no longer tell genes apart, the count evidence still does. Nor does this rest on the model alone: independent data support the count evidence in liver and testis and, in a pre-specified test, {Delta}[a] in liver. With both coordinates, one can ask whether another species uses a gene as humans do, the premise of every animal model of a disease gene or drug target.

papers.title: Fast, accurate construction of multiple sequence alignments from protein language embeddings
papers.abstract: Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) is a foundational task in computational biology, underpinning protein structure prediction, evolutionary analysis, and domain annotation. Traditional MSA algorithms rely on pairwise amino acid substitution matrices derived from conserved protein families. While effective for aligning closely related sequences, these scoring schemes struggle in the low-identity ``twilight zone.'' Here, we present a new approach for constructing MSAs leveraging amino acid embeddings generated by protein language models (PLMs), which capture rich evolutionary and contextual information from massive and diverse sequence datasets. We introduce a windowed reciprocal-weighted embedding similarity metric that is surprisingly effective in identifying corresponding amino acids across sequences. Building on this metric, we develop ARIES (Alignment via RecIprocal Embedding Similarity), an algorithm that constructs a PLM-generated template embedding and aligns each sequence to this template via dynamic time warping in order to build a global MSA. Across diverse benchmark datasets, ARIES achieves higher accuracies than existing state-of-the-art approaches, especially in low-identity regimes where traditional methods degrade, while scaling almost linearly with the number of sequences to be aligned. Together, these results provide the first large-scale demonstration of the power of PLMs for accurate and scalable MSA construction across protein families of varying sizes and levels of similarity, highlighting the potential of PLMs to transform comparative sequence analysis.

papers.title: Deep Lineage: Single-cell lineage tracing and fate inference using deep learning.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and lineage tracing techniques have provided valuable insights into the temporal changes in gene expression during development, tumor progression, and disease onset. However, there are few computational methods available to analyze this information to help understand multicellular dynamics. We introduce Deep Lineage, a deep-learning method for analyzing time-series single-cell RNA sequencing with matched lineage tracing data. Our method accurately predicts early cell fate biases and gene expression profiles at different time points within a clone, surpassing existing methods in fate prediction accuracy. We further validate our model using LineageSim, a fate-aware lineage simulator, demonstrating robustness to technical noise such as barcode dropout and clone misidentification. Additionally, we apply Deep Lineage to in silico perturbations in cellular reprogramming and hematopoiesis to identify key genes and pathways associated with cell fate determination and propose testable perturbation hypotheses for experimental follow-up.

papers.title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise.
papers.abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

papers.title: A universal deep-learning model for zinc finger design enables transcription factor reprogramming
papers.abstract: zinc finger (ZF) domains engineered to bind specific target sequences in the genome provide an effective strategy for programmable regulation of gene expression, with many potential therapeutic applications. However, the structurally intricate engagement of ZF domains with DNA has made their design challenging. Here we describe the screening of 49 billion protein-DNA interactions and the development of a deep-learning model, ZFDesign, that solves ZF design for any genomic target. ZFDesign is a modern machine learning method that models global and target-specific differences induced by a range of library environments and specifically takes into account compatibility of neighboring fingers using a novel hierarchical transformer architecture. We demonstrate the versatility of designed ZFs as nucleases as well as activators and repressors by seamless reprogramming of human transcription factors. These factors could be used to upregulate an allele of haploinsufficiency, downregulate a gain-of-function mutation or test the consequence of regulation of a single gene as opposed to the many genes that a transcription factor would normally influence.

papers.title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.

papers.title: PhageLysClass: Evidence-aware classification of phage lytic proteins using protein language models
papers.abstract: Phage lytic proteins are promising antibacterial and biotechnological candidates, yet uncertain annotations, modular architectures, and class imbalance complicate sequence-based classification. We developed PhageLysClass, an evidence-aware framework for recognizing lytic proteins and distinguishing Endolysins, Depolymerases, and virion-associated lytic enzymes. From 442,329 unique phage sequences, including 11,867 evidence-supported positives, we defined distinct candidate non-target, unlabeled, and challenge populations. Seven supervised and two positive-unlabeled tasks were evaluated across factorial redundancy and train-test homology conditions, yielding 2,240 and 768 experiments, respectively. Redundancy reduction influenced generalization more strongly than homology separation, with non-additive interactions between them. ESM2-T30 consistently outperformed alternative representations and supported a hierarchical classifier achieving approximately 0.89 MCC under strict R30/S30 conditions in the selected, pre-refitting benchmark. Applied without retraining to 77,897 sequences across three collections, PhageLysClass combined predictions with physicochemical and geometric contextualization, highlighting Depolymerase-like candidates among structurally ambiguous proteins while distinguishing reference-supported assignments from extrapolation.

papers.title: An Explainable and Scalable Hierarchical Tensor Framework for Integrating Multi-Omics and Digital Pathomics
papers.abstract: Background: Precision oncology requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and pathology data, yet many fusion models offer limited biologically grounded interpretability and struggle with missing modalities. Methods: We present Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (HIT-Fuse), integrating six modalities: somatic copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, RPPA protein abundance, and vision transformer-derived pathomics across four TCGA cohorts (glioma, lung adenocarcinoma, breast, and kidney cancer). Modality-specific autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs, followed by two-stage CP tensor decomposition. Missing latent modalities are reconstructed using clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts and retrain downstream models. A mathematical traceback mechanism enables global and local xAI attributions. Results: HIT-Fuse identifies distinct latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, both with complete and reconstructed modalities. Cohort expansion yields cohort-specific gains, including a 56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma. Biological validation against DepMap CRISPR screens, miRTarBase and RPPA annotations supports decoded drivers across all four cohorts. Essential gene rates range from 6.2% in glioma to 7.6% in lung cancer; example drivers include ANAPC11, SNRPD1, PLK1 and RPL14. Of decoded miRNAs, 71-92% have miRTarBase regulatory support, while 77-84% of selected genes are covered in DepMap. Conclusions: HIT-Fuse combines hierarchical tensor fusion, missing-modality reconstruction and traceable attributions to support interpretable multi-omics and digital pathology-based cancer prognosis across heterogeneous cohorts.

papers.title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.

papers.title: Dali server: structural unification of protein families
papers.abstract: Protein structure is key to understanding biological function. Structure comparison deciphers deep phylogenies, providing insight into functional conservation and functional shifts during evolution. Until recently, structural coverage of the protein universe was limited by the cost and labour involved in experimental structure determination. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning revolutionized structural bioinformatics by providing accurate structural models of numerous protein families for which no structural information existed. The Dali server for 3D protein structure comparison is widely used by crystallographers to relate new structures to pre-existing ones. Here, we report two most recent upgrades to the web server: (i) the foldomes of key organisms in the AlphaFold Database (version 1) are searchable by Dali, (ii) structural alignments are annotated with protein families. Using these new features, we discovered a novel functionally diverse subgroup within the WRKY/GCM1 clan. This was accomplished by linking the structurally characterized SWI/SNF and NAM families as well as the structural models of the CG-1 family and uncharacterized proteins to the structure of Gti1/Pac2, a previously known member of the WRKY/GCM1 clan. The Dali server is available at http://ekhidna2.biocenter.helsinki.fi/dali. This website is free and open to all users and there is no login requirement.

papers.title: Learning the limits of protein structure models with NMR chemical shifts
papers.abstract: Protein foundation models are intended to implicitly learn the chemical rules underlying protein function. However, systematically evaluating what biochemistry these models have learned remains difficult, as most downstream tasks lack experimental data fine-grained enough to expose their failure modes. NMR chemical shifts fill this gap: as direct per-atom reporters of local chemical environment, they offer a sensitive probe of structure-based representations. In this work, we present a systematically curated chemical shift dataset designed to minimize experimental confounders. We use it to benchmark diverse protein foundation models in their ability to predict backbone 15N chemical shifts, atoms that are known to be sensitive to many effects. The largest error across all models is in core residues with evidence of fast-timescale dynamics, which we investigate mechanistically using molecular dynamics simulations. Given the biological relevance of structured dynamic regions, we trained a new model based on the best of these embeddings, SLAE, to predict its own error. SLAE-ERR achieves a mean absolute error of 0.76 ppm for predicting error. Together, we hope that the datasets, evaluation tasks, and models presented here are sources of guidance for protein design model improvement.

papers.title: A disease-contextualized atlas of proteome-scale molecular influences of natural products
papers.abstract: Understanding the system-wide molecular effects of natural products remains challenging because chemical knowledge is fragmented, proteomic coverage is incomplete, and experimental perturbation data are scarce, particularly for multicomponent medicinal herbs. Here we present an integrative framework for modeling molecular influences of natural compounds and medicinal herbs in disease-specific contexts. We harmonized three herbal medicine databases to establish a standardized atlas of 46,422 chemical entities, 12,459 medicinal herbs, and 156,588 herb-compound associations. We integrated high-confidence protein-protein interactions with proteomic and transcriptomic data to reconstruct molecular networks across nine cancers. By prioritizing protein-level evidence and using transcriptomic associations to extend coverage, these networks capture disease-associated interaction rewiring beyond differential expression. We coupled AI-inferred compound-target interactions with signed random walks with restart to model the propagation of molecular influences from sparse direct targets to directional, genome-scale network profiles. Using gastric cancer as an in-depth case study, we generated profiles for 45,418 compounds across 16,899 molecular nodes and explored multicomponent herbal interventions. We further applied the framework to eight additional cancers and retrospectively compared selected profiles with published drug-perturbation proteomics. This atlas provides a scalable basis for systems-level modeling of natural-product interventions and mechanism-guided drug discovery.

papers.title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
papers.abstract: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants. Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.

papers.title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
papers.abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

papers.title: DBAASP V4: condition-resolved bioactivity and chemical structures for data-driven peptide and peptidomimetic discovery.
papers.abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.

papers.title: Towards Robust Automated Mouse Scratching Behavior Detection for Itch Research
papers.abstract: Quantification of mouse scratching behavior is essential for preclinical itch research. However, manual video annotation is labor-intensive, and automated detection remains challenging in terms of accuracy and generalizability. We present Scratch-AID+, a computational framework dedicated to automated mouse scratching detection, including a diverse and progressive set of model families and learning strategies: classic ResNet-based detectors, task-adaptive fine-tuning of video foundation models, and in-context learning of advanced multimodal large language models. To simulate real-world use cases, we benchmark on a public dataset containing annotated video recordings from a source laboratory with additional cross-laboratory videos for independent testing, and we explore different data preprocessing and training configurations. We find that classic models suffer severe performance degradation on external data under our realistic setting with sparse scratching events. In contrast, fine-tuned video foundation models substantially improve the generalizability, achieving significantly better detection performance. Furthermore, frozen multimodal large language models demonstrate promising out-of-the-box ability using only few-shot demonstrations.We also report the effects of different video preprocessing strategies and ablations. Our findings highlight the improved performance and generalizability of the adapted foundation models for automated scratching behavior analysis and shed light on the real-world deployment of such detectors. Our code is publicly available at github.com/PennShenLab/scratch-aid-plus.

papers.title: Evaluating generative models for structure-based drug discovery from de novo design to lead optimization.
papers.abstract: Advances in protein structure prediction have created opportunities for structure-based drug design, yet translating structural knowledge into actionable small-molecule ligands remains difficult. Existing benchmarks often use simplified datasets and computational surrogates that poorly capture the heterogeneity and constraints of real-world drug discovery. We introduce MolGenBench, a comprehensive benchmark for de novo molecular generation and hit-to-lead optimization built on a large, structurally diverse dataset. Evaluation of 17 leading methods reveals persistent limitations, including weak virtual-screening performance, limited coverage of target-specific bioactive space, frequent high-risk structural motifs, poor target awareness, and reduced generalization to unseen proteins. Although some models improve three-dimensional conformation generation, they still struggle to produce active molecules reliably. MolGenBench provides standardized data, metrics, and analyses that connect structural prediction with practical molecular design and guide the development of more effective structure-based generative models.

papers.title: How Much Can AI Virtual Cells Gain from Unified Perturbational Modeling?
papers.abstract: Predicting how individual cells respond to perturbations is a central task in artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC) modeling. However, integrating perturbation datasets is challenging because they differ in measured gene sets, perturbation types and cellular contexts. Existing AIVC predictors are typically developed for specific settings, limiting their applicability across heterogeneous datasets. Here, we investigate the extent to which AIVC predictors can benefit from unified perturbational modeling (UPM), a novel paradigm designed to integrate heterogeneous Perturb-seq datasets into a single predictive model. To this end, we introduce three unification modules into a variational autoencoder (VAE)-based AIVC predictor to address these sources of heterogeneity: gene-channel alignment, shared perturbation encoding, and joint embedding of gene expression and identity. We systematically evaluate and validate the individual contributions of these modules. Building on UPM, we assemble a dataset of 110 million cells spanning over 22,000 genes, four perturbation types and 76 cellular contexts, and use 89.7 million cells from 71 contexts to train a unified AIVC predictor with more than one billion parameters. Across genetic perturbation benchmarks, UPM achieves the highest PES and gene-wise response correlation among the evaluated models. It also improves all four evaluation metrics over State on the five held-out Tahoe-100M cell lines and over Stack on the cytokine benchmark. UPM also improves combinatorial perturbation prediction relative to specialized predictors. In the HSC application, our model achieves a 40.0% improvement in accuracy on a downstream task involving the recapitulation of effects induced by the knockdown of hepatic stellate cell (HSC)-related targets. Our implementation is openly available at https://github.com/youlab2025/UPM.

papers.title: Prediction and Dissection of Nitrogenase Activity Based on Protein Sequences using Dual Descriptor
papers.abstract: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, but its activity differs markedly among natural sequences, and conventional wet-laboratory screening suffers from low throughput and long turnaround times. Existing computational methods have partially alleviated this bottleneck, yet most of them rely on protein embeddings obtained from protein language models together with features such as gene expression, and their interpretability analyses mostly stop at the level of feature contribution. Here we present CarmnaDD, a purely sequence-driven framework built on the dual descriptor (DD): two learnable components, the composition weight map (CWM) and the position weight function (PWF), jointly generate a position-resolved description N(k), so that activity can be predicted without any prior knowledge beyond the sequence. On the same dataset used by Carmna, CarmnaDD attains R2 = 0.60 for regression and AUC = 0.94 and F1 = 0.86 for classification, better than our previous Carmna, which integrates multiple features. Interpretability analysis shows that the amplitude of the periodic terms of the PWF decreases as the rank increases, indicating that the positional encoding strategy adapts to the rank; the high-weight 3-mer fragments in the CWM are significantly enriched in polar uncharged residues, which corroborates the SHAP-based conclusion of Carmna; sliding-window scanning identifies fragments significantly associated with activity (FDR < 0.05), and the strongest window displays a D-X-E pattern with conserved flanks and a polymorphic center, sequences carrying R at the central position showing the highest activity; conservation is significantly negatively correlated ({rho} = -0.30) with description intensity. Mapping the key windows onto the protein structure shows that four highly correlated windows converge on the nucleotide-binding interface and the conformational-transmission/protein-docking interface of NifH. These results provide a purely sequence-based framework for nitrogenase activity prediction that balances performance and interpretability.

papers.title: A Whole-Blood Four-Gene Panel Distinguishes Pediatric Crohn's Disease from Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Crohn's disease and disorders of gut-brain interaction present with overlapping symptoms, and distinguishing them often requires endoscopy. We assessed whether the whole-blood transcriptome at presentation distinguishes these conditions and reflects disease activity. Methods: In a prospective two-center cohort, whole-blood RNA sequencing was performed in 425 treatment-naive participants aged 5 to 25 years (112 Crohn's disease, 313 disorders of gut-brain interaction). Differential expression was modeled for diagnosis and, within Crohn's disease, for the Pediatric Crohn's Disease Activity Index. Co-expression modules were integrated with protein-protein interaction networks, and machine learning distilled network genes into a diagnostic panel, evaluated internally and in an independent pediatric cohort. Results: Of 1,095 diagnosis-associated genes, 377 were also associated with disease activity, all with concordant direction. Five co-expression networks were perturbed, spanning neutrophil degranulation, hemostasis, interferon signaling, and T-cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte programs. A 4-gene panel (PSTPIP2, CLIC4, CACNB4, GZMK) drawn from 4 networks achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of up to 0.96 in held-out samples and up to 0.93 externally, with external specificity and positive predictive value of up to 0.95 and 0.93, respectively. The panel matched or exceeded every single-network panel with fewer genes, and minimally active Crohn's disease overlapped transcriptionally with disorders of gut-brain interaction. Conclusions: At diagnosis, Crohn's disease is distinguished from disorders of gut-brain interaction by a systemic signature of neutrophil and platelet activation and lymphocyte depletion that scales with disease activity. A 4-gene whole-blood panel may help prioritize symptomatic children for endoscopy and warrants prospective validation.

papers.title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study
papers.abstract: Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. Objectives: To leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods 236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. Results Top features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGFA, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK STAT, T cell, and Toll like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. Conclusions Across cohorts, JAK STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK STAT directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.
